Subject: Dedicated renewal: recommended reserved-pool increase & throughput plan

Hi Alyssa —

Thanks again for the time last week. As you start preparing for the Jan 15 renewal, I pulled together a conservative capacity recommendation and an initial cost/throughput model for Northstar’s Dedicated pool. Attachments: northstar_capacity_plan_v3.pdf and northstar_cost_model_q1-2027.xlsx (summary below).

Quick context and ask:
- Current committed capacity: 8 GPUs (active since 2025 renewal) serving a mix of LLM workloads (inference for search ranking, chat assistants, and embeddings-heavy vectorization jobs).
- Observed steady-state avg QPS (across models): ~120 QPS during business hours; peak bursts up to 270 QPS for short windows during product launches.
- Average response size: ~420 tokens per call; 95th pct response token length ~1,100 tokens for a small subset of requests.

Forecast assumptions (conservative):
- Usage growth: +35% net QPS by the next renewal season (driven by two feature launches and 3 product teams onboarded)
- Burst multiplier: expected bursts to increase proportionally — we plan for 2x short-term headroom above steady-state.

Redwood recommendation summary:
- Reservation: increase reserved pool from 8 -> 14 GPUs (add 6 GPUs) to cover steady-state growth + baseline headroom.
- Burst capacity: allow 6 GPU burstable buffer (can be met via autoscale credits or short-term burst nodes in the Dedicated plan).
- Target SLO: 99th percentile tail latency <= 300ms for responses <= 500 tokens; graceful degradation + model-fallback for longer-generation workloads.
- Rollout: phased upgrade — commit 4 GPUs at renewal start (Jan 15), add final 2 GPUs after launch window (by Mar 1) contingent on telemetry.

Why 6 additional GPUs? (summary math — details in the attached PDF):
- Effective per-GPU steady throughput (mixed-model, quantized inference) measured on your workload: ~18 sustained QPS for median 420-token requests.
- Projected steady QPS after growth: ~162 QPS -> requires ~9 GPUs purely for steady-state (162/18 ≈ 9).
- Allowing for 50% buffer for spikes, cache misses, and larger generations moves us to ~14 GPUs.

Next steps / asks from your side:
1) Can Miguel or procurement confirm any constraints around reserved vs burstable billing? (cc’d Miguel + procurement).
2) Can you share the model mix breakdown (percent of requests by model family) so we can tighten the recommendation?
3) If you’re comfortable, we’ll prepare an updated quote and a phased MUP (mutual action plan) for signatures.

I’ll loop in Karthik (inference ops) for the technical sizing notes in my follow-up.

Thanks —

Alyssa — thanks for the quick reply and the model mix. I’ve sketched a short technical note below and pulled Karthik in for the per-model latency estimate.

Technical sizing note (ballpark, for discussion):
- Per-GPU sustained capacity estimate: 18 QPS for your median 420-token requests (this is conservative; higher with batching/caching optimizations).
- Embeddings / encoder-heavy calls: these are cheaper and can be routed to smaller instance classes or pooled to reduce pressure on the main generator pool — we expect embeddings to consume ~1/3 of a generator GPU’s capacity if routed separately.
- Long-form summarizations (1k+ tokens): these burn KV cache and increase tail latency; plan to route those to a pair of GPUs with higher sequence-optimized kernels (we recommend pinning an instance pair for these heavy runs).

Per-model 99th pct projection (under 14 GPUs, mixed routing + 2 dedicated seq-optimized GPUs):
- 13B chat family (60%): expected 99th pct ~ 220–320ms for responses <= 500 tokens (dependent on batching).
- Embeddings (30%): 99th pct ~ 80–140ms (short tokens).
- Long-form summarization (10%): 99th pct ~ 700–1,200ms on 1k+ tokens unless responses are sharded / fallback to a smaller model for tails.

Operational recommendation:
- Phased activation: enable 4 additional GPUs at renewal + 2 more after launch telemetry (as suggested).
- Reserve 2 GPUs as sequence-optimized (pinning) for long-form jobs.
- Configure request routing policy: route short embeddings to a separate pool (cost saving) and route long-form to pinned GPUs.

Karthik — can you confirm the above latency bands with a short perf-scan on our staging harness? If we can attach the staging run results to the quote, that will help Alyssa’s product team sign off.

I’ll prepare an updated quote and proposed MUP once Karthik confirms the perf numbers.

—Priyom
